prize_parts.citation: for showing how technological change and import competition reshape labour demand, wage inequality and the adjustment of local labour markets

statement.case_for: B022 combines a first-order question with credible identification. The task-based account of technology and the China-shock studies explain who gains and loses from technological and trade change, why adjustment in local labour markets can be slow and costly, and why this matters for policy and public debate. The empirical designs are transparent and have been widely replicated, extended and contested over more than a decade. Contested work has been tested more thoroughly than untested work, and the central findings on wages, employment and regional adjustment have held up in several settings. Seen from my own field, the work also made it measurable how economic dislocation connects to political and social outcomes, which is a large part of its reach beyond labour economics. Support is broad in the opening rankings, but I rest my case on the research design and the explanatory payoff, not on the count. I now propose three names instead of my opening two. The China-shock evidence is a joint Autor-Dorn-Hanson body of work, and a citation about technology and trade shocks is more accurately credited to the trio.
statement.case_against: The credit allocation is the main weakness. The task-based framework has contributors outside the credited set, including Acemoglu, Levy and Murnane, and Katz is credited on the ballot for the earlier skill-premium literature. A citation that mentions technology could therefore be read as under-crediting others, and a citation limited to trade shocks would leave the task framework unrecognised. The magnitude and persistence of the China-shock effects are still debated, and shift-share designs face identification critiques. The theme is also close to the 2024 prize on technology, growth and institutions. I weigh these concerns against the strength of the evidence, and they argue for a carefully worded citation, not for a different candidate.

responses.point: Enflo ranks B022 first and proposes Autor, Hanson and Dorn. She argues the work links measurement, causal design and policy relevance, and that the China-shock trio is the cleanest basis for a three-person limit. She also flags continuing debate over the persistence and size of the effects.
responses.response: I agree on the trio and have revised my opening proposal accordingly. I had treated Dorn as a secondary co-author, but his role in the China-shock papers is not secondary, and seniority is not a scientific criterion. I also share her view that the persistence debate is a real uncertainty. I would add that it concerns the size and duration of the effects, not whether the adjustment costs exist, so it argues for a careful citation, not against the award. Her open question is whether the task framework or the trade-shock evidence is the more prize-worthy core. I think a citation naming both shocks to labour demand, technology and trade, avoids having to choose, but I accept it leaves the credit to the task framework's other originators unresolved.

responses.point: Hassler places B022 fifth and proposes only Autor and Hanson. He sees credit as blurred between task-based theory (Acemoglu-Autor) and the empirical China-shock work, and notes thematic proximity to the 2024 prize.
responses.response: I share his attribution concern and opened with the same two names for a similar reason. After reading the other openings, I think a two-person prize would leave out a co-originator of the best-identified part of the work, and the China-shock papers are not separable from Dorn. On the 2024 proximity, I would treat the prize as honouring distinct findings. The 2024 work concerned the causal effect of institutions on long-run prosperity, while B022 concerns how technology and trade shocks redistribute within economies and across regions. They share a broad theme but not the core result. The overlap with Acemoglu's task work is real, which is why I want the citation tied to the empirical evidence on labour demand and adjustment, not to the theory of tasks.

responses.point: Krusell ranks B029 first and B047 second. He regards B047 as mature, concentrated and coherent in credit, and as overlapping the 2024 prize in theme but not in core contribution. He also notes that the identification of the empirical constitutional results is debated.
responses.response: I agree that B047 is coherent, and it is why I keep it as an alternative. I disagree that the 2024 overlap is merely thematic. The Committee has just recognised the causal effect of institutions on prosperity. Awarding the formal and empirical study of constitutions and electoral rules so soon could be read as a second prize on adjacent ground. That is a judgment about timing, not about merit. The cross-country identification of constitutional effects is, in my view, weaker than the identification in B022. I rank B029 lower because I cannot weigh the methodological claims of empirical IO as well as the labour-market evidence, so I will not argue for or against the merits of Pakes, Berry and Levinsohn.

responses.point: Andersson ranks B007 first. He argues that Grossman and Helpman are clear originators of the political-economy framework for trade policy, that attribution to the pair is clean, and that maturity is very high. He also notes that empirical support is mixed and that Helpman appears in B012.
responses.response: I agree on the attribution, which is the cleanest on the shortlist, and it is why B007 is my first alternative. Where we differ is the weight. His own uncertainties show that the empirical support for the lobbying model's precise predictions is mixed, and the committee may prefer to frame a Helpman award around heterogeneity or growth instead. That framing question is unresolved, and the unresolved framing is what keeps B007 below B022 for me. A prize whose citation the Committee cannot yet agree on is riskier than one whose main difficulty is the credit allocation within a defined body of work.

responses.point: Boppart ranks B012 first and proposes Helpman and Melitz. He argues the heterogeneous-firm framework is a well-confirmed workhorse and that trade has not been recognised since 2008, which makes the timing favourable.
responses.response: I take the trade-timing argument seriously, and the opening rankings show that B012 and B022 are linked through trade. I do not see B012 and B022 as competing for the same space. B012 is a contribution to trade theory and quantification. B022 concerns the distributional and labour-market consequences of trade and technology shocks. If the Committee wants to recognise trade, B012 is the more direct route, and I would not stand in its way. I rank B022 higher because it brings credible empirical designs to a question about people and places that the theoretical framework in B012 does not address. This is a judgment about explanatory reach, and I cannot establish it from the evidence supplied.

uncertainties: Whether a citation can recognise the empirical labour-market work without understating the task framework's other originators (Acemoglu, Levy, Murnane) who are outside the credited set.
How much the long-run size and persistence of the China-shock effects, and the identification critiques of shift-share designs, should reduce the weight on the findings.
Whether the Committee views the proximity to the 2024 prize as a reason for delay.
Whether Katz should be included on the ballot's own credited list. I have not proposed him, but I cannot rule out a defensible case from the supplied evidence.
My recollection of the contributions is general knowledge and has not been independently verified against the literature.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent for the preferred configuration (B022) from the supplied profile. For the alternative B047, the profile lists a co-authored Governance paper on corruption as a collective-action problem with a 'Persson' and Rothstein, without a first name. I cannot establish from the supplied evidence whether this is Torsten Persson, so my opening statement that I co-authored with Persson was stated more firmly than the profile supports. My field of comparative political institutions also overlaps closely with B047. I also hold the same university affiliation, Stockholm University, as colleagues in a different department. I disclose these without adjudicating them.
